title: Husky Robotics — Hand Board
summary: Wrote bare-metal C on STM32G4 to control a robotic hand on the rover with stepper motors, solenoids, and a laser, coordinated over the rover's FDCAN bus.
details:
The hand board is the firmware for the gripper on Husky Robotics' rover. It has to control a stepper motor, some solenoids, and a laser, and it has to talk reliably to the rest of the rover over CAN.

How it works together:
An STM32G4 chip runs everything. It drives the stepper motor through a DRV8825 driver, controls the solenoids, and controls the laser's brightness with PWM. It also sends and receives CAN messages to the rover's main computer (NVIDIA Jetson).

Challenges I faced:
• Motor noise was causing false signals on other pins when the stepper drew high current. I fixed this by adding filtering in firmware and cleaning up the ground layout on the board.
• The DRV8825 doesn't report the motor's position, so I wrote code to count steps in real time and added limit switches (with interrupts) so the arm knows when it's hit its physical limits.
• The laser flickered at low brightness. I found this was a PWM resolution problem and fixed it by switching from 8-bit to 10-bit timer resolution, which meant recalculating the timer settings and retesting brightness levels.
• I made sure my code never blocked for too long, since a teammate's CAN heartbeat and emergency-stop logic depended on messages going out on time.
tech: C, STM32G474, FDCAN, PWM, DRV8825, Stepper Motors

title: Vaakya — Wearable Real-Time Captioning
summary: Built the real time captioning pipeline for Vaakya, AI glasses that caption speech for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. Uses an offline speech to text model, runs on two threads to keep it fast, and shows captions on an AR display.
details:
Vaakya is AI glasses that show live captions of what people are saying, built for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. I built the software and the hardware integration for it.

How it works:
The mic picks up audio and puts it in a queue. One thread takes that audio and runs it through Vosk, which is an offline speech to text model, and turns it into text. A second thread runs the display at 60 FPS and shows the captions on the AR display. I split it into two threads so the captions don't stutter, since the display doesn't have to wait on the model to finish.

Just showing whatever the model returns looked bad, since short pieces of text came back fast and looked spammy as separate lines. So I added logic to merge nearby pieces into one caption, and made old captions disappear after a few seconds instead of piling up. I also had to tune the latency differently depending on the hardware, since what worked on a Mac was too fast for a Raspberry Pi.

Everything runs locally, so it doesn't need internet and nothing gets sent anywhere.

Why I'm building this:
While playing cricket, I met someone who was deaf and wanted to join us, and it was hard to include him. I wanted to build something that actually lets people like him be part of the conversation instead of just watching it happen.

The project got selected for the Lavin x Anthropic entrepreneurship program, and I raised a $2K seed round after pitching it to UW's Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship in front of industry people and investors.
tech: Python, Vosk STT, Raspberry Pi, Docker

title: GPS-Navigating Mecanum Rover
summary: Building an autonomous holonomic rover on RP2040 with custom GPS/IMU drivers and mecanum drive control, currently in testing ahead of a club-wide rollout.
details:
The project started with a practical question: how do we test controls without breaking real hardware every time something is wrong? I built a testing rover around an RP2040, which is cheap, so making mistakes on it won't make us lose our minimal budget.

The rover gets its position from a NEO-6M GPS module and its heading from a BNO055 IMU. I wrote custom UART and I2C drivers for both since we didn't have the budget to buy something off-the-shelf. GPS updates are slow and noisy, so the firmware combines that with the IMU's faster heading data to get more reliable data.

The rover has four wheels, and each wheel has its own motor, so it can strafe sideways or spin in place. I worked out the kinematic math by hand so I'd actually understand why a given wheel-speed combo produces a given motion.

This project is currently in its testing phase and will be deployed before the end of the quarter so new club members can use it.
tech: C, RP2040, UART, I2C, NEO-6M GPS, BNO055 IMU

title: Embassy — STM32 HAL Fixes
summary: Diagnosed and fixed a flash erase bug and a related bounds-check bug on chips with non-contiguous flash banks, and root-caused an I2C slave NVIC interrupt hang from a community bug report.
details:
I contribute to embassy-rs, the async embedded framework a lot of the Rust embedded community builds on, and three bugs I chased down there turned into merged fixes.

The first was a flash erase bug on the STM32G473CB caused by non-contiguous flash banks — the chip has a physical gap between Bank1 and Bank2 that the erase logic didn't account for. I fixed it by correcting the bank-relative page indexing, and added an async bank-mode sanity check so the driver fails early if the configured bank mode doesn't match the chip's actual option bytes, instead of silently misbehaving.

While I was in there I found a related bug: the flash bounds check was rejecting valid Bank2 addresses on the same non-contiguous-bank chips, because it validated offsets against total flash size instead of the chip's true addressable span. I fixed that by bounding offsets against the real address range.

The third came from a community bug report describing an I2C slave interrupt hang. I traced it back to an unbound interrupt handler that new_blocking() was leaving enabled — since blocking mode never registers a handler, a real interrupt firing had nowhere to go and the slave hung. I fixed the masking logic so blocking mode no longer enables interrupts it doesn't use, and closed a separate ADDRIE race condition against the interrupt handler while root-causing it.

title: Microsoft CFU Protocol — Rust Firmware
summary: Identified and fixed a code-duplication risk in Microsoft's open-source CFU firmware service, simplifying response logic shared between the Buffer and Splitter components.
details:
I contributed to the Open Device Partnership, a Microsoft-affiliated open-source project, working in production Rust firmware on the Component Firmware Update (CFU) protocol — the service responsible for getting firmware updates safely onto a device.

While reading through the CFU service, I identified a code-duplication risk: the Buffer and Splitter components each maintained their own independent copy of the validation logic for invalid version and content rejection. Two independent copies of the same logic is exactly the kind of thing that quietly drifts out of sync over time — a fix applied to one copy with no reason to touch the other. I simplified the response logic by moving that common code into a shared module used by both components, so there's one implementation instead of two that are supposed to agree.

title: Electric Skateboard
summary: Built a dual-motor electric skateboard with brushless DC hub motors and a VESC motor controller, powered by a custom 10S3P lithium-ion battery pack (36V, 7.8Ah).
details:
This one started as a personal project back in 2023 and I've kept coming back to it since. I built a dual-motor electric skateboard from the ground up — brushless DC hub motors for drive, and a VESC (Vedder Electronic Speed Controller) handling the motor control side, which is the same open-source controller a lot of the DIY e-skate community builds around.

The part I spent the most time getting right was the battery: a custom 10S3P lithium-ion pack — 10 cells in series for a 36V nominal pack voltage, 3 in parallel per group for capacity, landing at 7.8Ah total. Building a pack by hand means owning every part of that decision: cell selection, spot-welding the nickel strips, balancing taps for the BMS, and making sure the whole thing can deliver the current two hub motors actually pull under load without sagging or overheating. It's a good reminder that battery systems aren't just a spec on a datasheet — they're a physical thing you have to build correctly or it becomes a safety problem, not just a performance one.
